correctness.rationale: Every convex noncrossing tree is one of the 54264 six-edge subsets of the 21 edges, with acyclicity and cyclic crossing constraints. I independently enumerated this complete 54264 candidate set using a distinct DSU/crossing implementation, obtaining exactly 1428 admissible edge masks. An independently coded 21-stage exact integer Walsh-Hadamard transform across all 2097152 edge characters gave exactly 160484 zero multipliers, least positive |W|=4, and 14 two-edge zero masks; Parseval sum 2097152*1428 matched. A second 21-stage exact transform of the nonzero-frequency indicator gave absolute sum 312904152, hence projection convolution l1/linfty norm 312904152/2097152=39113019/262144. The analytic argument for universal multiple-of-four from even single-edge incidence and two-edge orbit cancellation was reconstructed. This is exhaustive finite integer arithmetic, not extrapolation to other polygon sizes.

evidence: Full Flajolet-Noy primary PDF gives general noncrossing graph/tree enumeration; Wettstein gives crossing-free graph enumeration algorithms.
broader_coverage.reasoning: General enumeration over all n or all geometric graphs does not by itself imply the heptagon 21-variable Walsh zero histogram or endpoint Fourier-projection absolute sum. A hidden specialization of a joint edge polynomial remains an explicit risk.

value.rationale: Convex noncrossing spanning trees form a classical and naturally enumerated geometric combinatorial class. The first exact parity-cancellation orbit, complete character nullity and sharp endpoint projector norm measure real information loss/recovery for the edge-incidence orbit; they are not implied by the count 1428 or vertex-degree refinements. A nontrivial finite exact invariant is independently useful even without an all-n theorem.

limitations: A fixed n=7 exact result; no general polygon-size theorem.
One route to finite exact integer certificate was independently recomputed; supplied second route inspected but its saved result alone was not accepted as proof.
The complete finite integer Fourier transform spans every character and cannot be dismissed as a sample; no larger-n classification is claimed.
